The titling of famous paintings creates persistent confusion because artworks are often known by multiple names. Popular titles differ from official ones. Artists did not always title their own works. And translations and scholarly renaming complicate identification even further.

Many Old Masters didn't give their paintings formal titles at all. Titles were assigned later by curators, collectors, or art historians based on the subject matter or provenance. So the same painting may have several different names. Official museum titles often differ completely from popular names. Edvard Munch's work is famously called The Scream, but its formal Norwegian title is Skrik, which means Shriek or Cry.

Translation introduces real ambiguity. Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon translates as The Young Ladies of Avignon, or possibly The Avignon Prostitutes, depending on how you interpret the French word "demoiselles." Some paintings are titled after their owners or locations rather than their content. Velázquez's The Rokeby Venus is named for its former location at Rokeby Hall, not for its subject matter. Restoration and cleaning of paintings sometimes reveals original signatures or dated inscriptions that affect how a work is identified. Reattribution of authorship can change the registered title.

Common mistakes happen all the time. People call Kandinsky's Composition VII by vague names like "abstract painting." They confuse Franz Hals's Laughing Cavalier with Rembrandt. They refer to paintings by generic descriptions instead of proper titles—like "the one with the melting clocks" instead of using the actual name.
